doc.title: Sol Yaged interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000

title: Racial mixing in bands and Goodman's integrated groups
summary: Sol says he always played with black and white musicians, and recalls Goodman's integrated bands and Charlie Christian.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When did it become let’s say acceptable to mix racially in the groups in New York City? Was there ever a problem for you?

Not that I know of. I have been playing with black and white musicians all my life. I started, and I have pictures to prove it, I’ll show them to you. One time I was on the stage with Jimmy Jones on piano and John Levy on bass. I’ll show you the pictures. Tim are those gentlemen still outside? See if they’re outside please. I never had a problem. I played on the stage with Sidney Bechet. I played on the stage with Wilbur DeParis, Sidney DeParis, J.C. Higginbotham. Didn’t bother me. I know Benny Goodman had a difficult time when he first started in the 30’s.
Maybe you should make a call down to the front desk.
Their names are Sal and Arthur. Thank you Tim Hicks, thank you, sir.
Did the guy near the elevator stop you?
The security guard. And I gave him the information. He was very nice. In fact there were two security men there. You speak very nice by the way.

You have a very easy way of speaking. I like talking to you. See when Benny Goodman first started out with his band, 1935, he had Teddy Wilson with him and in 1936 Lionel Hampton. When he played certain places they didn’t want — he said this is my band, take me as it is. He may have said this I don’t know, but it’s like saying what you see is what you get. I mean he didn’t delete Lionel Hampton because he was black and he didn’t let Cootie Williams out because he was black and he didn’t leave Teddy Wilson out of the band because he was black. You know Benny Goodman at one time had an all- black rhythm section, and I was there. He had Big Sid Catlett on drums, he had John Simmons on bass, he had Charlie Christian on guitar, and he had Fletcher Henderson on piano. And I was there when they were playing at Frank Daily’s Meadowbrook, Monk, in New Jersey. He had an all-black rhythm section. In fact I’ll even tell you he had a black saxophone player with him at that time, Budd Johnson. So he had his share of black musicians at one time, a full array.
That’s a real shame Charlie Christian didn’t last longer.
Did he cause quite a sensation with what he did?
Oh yeah. He was a very young man when he passed away, very, very young. I think he was like 23, 24 years old.
